item.title: 英メーガン妃の父親逮捕、子どもの性的虐待画像所持の疑い
item.description: ［ワシントン ６日 ロイター］ -
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
［ワシントン　６日　ロイター］ - 英国のヘンリー王子の妻メーガン妃の父親トーマス・マークル容疑者（８２）が６日、子どもの性的虐待画像を所持した疑いで逮捕、訴追された。画像はカリフォルニア州の貸倉庫から見つかり、裸の未成年の少女と容疑者が一緒に写った写真も含まれている。

パテル米連邦捜査局（ＦＢＩ）長官によると、容疑者はフロリダ州で連邦捜査官に身柄を拘束された。英紙デーリー・メールによると、容疑者は同州の介護施設に入所しており、車椅子を使用しているという。

パテル氏は声明で「罪のない子どもたちを標的にし、犯罪行為によってその純真さを奪おうとした疑いがある」と説明した。司法省によると、有罪となれば最高で禁錮２０年の刑が科される可能性がある。

容疑者は、フロリダ州タンパで連邦治安判事の前に初出廷した。ロサンゼルスの連邦検察当局の声明によると、判事は自宅拘禁と電子監視に従うことを条件に、裁判を待つ間の釈放を命じた。

声明によると、罪状認否はまだ行われておらず、数週間先になる見通し。

英王室とメーガン妃の広報担当者は、コメントの要請に応じなかった。

item.title: India in Final-Stage Talks to Expand Missile Sale to Philippines, Sources Say
item.description: India is in final-stage talks to expand its sale of supersonic cruise missiles to the Philippines, three sources with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters, as New Delhi nears completion of deliveries under a 2022 deal. The Philippines is expected to buy about five …
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded:
India is in final-stage talks to expand its sale of supersonic cruise missiles to the Philippines, three sources with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters, as New Delhi nears completion of deliveries under a 2022 deal.

The Philippines is expected to buy about five BrahMos systems, nearly 60 missiles in total, in a deal potentially worth $700 million to $800 million, two of the Indian sources said.

“Manila has shown interest again to procure about 5 systems of the BrahMos, and they now view India as a very reliable partner,” one Indian source said.

New Delhi’s latest likely deal with the Philippines, which is modernizing its military and strengthening coastal defenses as tensions rise in the disputed South China Sea, is much higher than the last $375 million order of BrahMos for naval use.

BrahMos, developed jointly by India and Russia, is among the world’s fastest cruise missiles and can be launched from land, sea and air platforms.

Arsenio Andolong, Philippines defense ministry spokesperson, told Reuters that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. had expressed his desire to acquire additional BrahMos missiles. Andolong did not offer more details.

Speaking virtually at the Delhi Defense Dialogue on Wednesday, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said the Philippines hoped to secure more BrahMos units and had shared a wish list with Indian authorities to tailor the system to the Philippine environment.

Reuters is the first to report the size and value of the deal.

The additional purchase comes at a time when Manila is building its military strength as tension escalates with Beijing over overlapping claims in the South China Sea, where the two countries have clashed in recent years.

India’s defence and foreign ministries, as well as missile maker BrahMos Aerospace, did not respond to requests for comment.

Interest in the BrahMos system has increased since last year’s four-day conflict between India and Pakistan, when India used the weapons system for the first time in battle.

In July, Delhi announced the supply of BrahMos missiles to Indonesia and has also signed a deal with Vietnam. It is in talks on the system with a number of other countries including UAE , Thailand, South Africa and Brazil.

India’s defense exports for the fiscal year to March reached 384.24 billion rupees ($4.11 billion), a jump of more than 62% from the same period the year before, government data showed.

FAST

WASHINGTON, Nov 7 : Environmental groups worldwide are using artificial intelligence to analyze climate data, track forest fires and count endangered wildlife – embracing a technology they also warn is driving a surge in electricity demand, water use and greenhouse-gas emissions. The contradiction is forcing these organizations to justify their AI use in carrying out missions to combat climate change or protect natural resources. "We recognize that AI can come with environmental costs, and we need to be thoughtful about how we use it," said Ali Swanson, AI lead at the US nonprofit Conservation International. "But at a time when the climate and biodiversity crises are becoming more urgent, AI can help us move faster and make better use of the information we're collecting." The group recently started using AI to assess hotspots detected by satellites and send real-time alerts to community forest patrols about potential wildfires in remote and environmentally sensitive parts of Cambodia.

Reuters interviewed 15 major environmental, conservation and development organizations about their AI use. All said they used the technology in some form and expressed concern about the environmental impact of the data centers powering it. The centers, filled with servers, can require vast amounts of electricity, along with water for cooling. It's a global dilemma for individuals, governments and industries balancing AI's benefits with its enormous risks. The tradeoffs likely will grab attention at the UN's COP31 climate conference this month, when host Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres wants major AI companies to publicly disclose their systems' environmental impacts. Researchers at the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health estimate the global data-center footprint could more than double by 2030, reaching a size about twice that of Jakarta, the Indonesian megalopolis. The International Energy Agency, meanwhile, estimates global data centers will consume about 945 terawatt-hours of electricity annually by 2030, producing the equivalent of more than 300 million metric tons of carbon dioxide. That's double current consumption and about equal to Japan's annual electricity use. The agency also projects that global data center water consumption will increase from about 560 billion liters (147.9 billion gallons) in 2023 to about 1.2 trillion liters (317 billion gallons) annually by 2030. Technology giants including Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet's Google have reported rising emissions linked in part to data center expansion, raising questions about their ability to meet their own long-term climate goals. Amazon told Reuters its artificial-intelligence products were among the most sustainable due to the company's purchases of low-carbon energy and its efforts to use power and water efficiently. Microsoft and Google didn't respond to requests for comment. BREAKTHROUGHS ONCE THOUGHT IMPOSSIBLE Many of the organizations that spoke to Reuters believe AI's benefits currently outweigh its costs because the technology is enabling work that was previously difficult, expensive or impossible. Kenya's Save the Elephants, a partner of the Wildlife Conservation Network, said it is using machine learning to improve population surveys and study elephant communication. Frank Pope, the group's chief executive, said an aerial survey of Kenya's largest protected area last year generated roughly 200,000 images that took nine people nine months to review manually. AI models trained on Nvidia's GeForce graphics platforms can now complete similar analyses in hours. "The results have been eye-opening," Pope said. "We found that human surveys were missing about a third of the elephants, roughly half of zebras and giraffes, and three-quarters of oryx populations." More accurate wildlife data can help secure financing for conservation, he said. "Ultimately, these tools make nature measurable and therefore investable," he said. "That's a critical transformation, if we're going to conserve biodiversity at scale." At the institute founded by the late conservation icon Jane Goodall, researchers are using AI to digitize decades of field notes about chimpanzee behavior in Tanzania's Gombe National Park. The project was once expected to take 13-15 years because the records were written by hand using the local Kiha language and scientific shorthand. Thanks to a tool developed with Amazon Web Services, the notes can now be scanned, translated and structured in minutes, slashing the time needed to about two years, said Lilian Pintea, the Jane Goodall Institute's vice president of conservation science. During her lifetime, Pintea said, Goodall supported the use of AI to advance conservation science, provided people remained firmly in control of how it was used. "AI technology should be seen as tools which are human-centered," Pintea said. LIMITING THE ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT Some organizations are experimenting with ways to limit the environmental impact of their AI use. The World Resources Institute (WRI), a research group that uses AI to accelerate its climate and environmental analyses, said it limits resource-intensive applications such as generating videos and images, while caching AI query results so identical searches don't need to be reprocessed. The US-based Nature Conservancy has adopted a similar approach. It uses AI to analyze video captured on commercial fishing vessels for information on how many fish of different species they catch. But instead of uploading huge numbers of videos to centralized data centers, it has installed AI-powered digital cameras to process information aboard the vessels, reducing energy use and data-transfer requirements, said Vienna Saccomanno, a senior scientist at the organization. "It takes a lot of engineering to make computation on the edge possible," she said. "This was worth it to reduce both our carbon footprint and deliver these sustainability insights." Greenpeace International said it, too, uses some AI tools, mainly because software platforms it relies upon include AI features. It's imposing internal guidelines emphasizing transparency, human oversight and "intentional" AI use, the group said. But it would prefer to sidestep the technology due to its environmental impacts and is pushing back hard on the data center buildout. "While other organizations are asking how to use AI responsibly, Greenpeace is asking whether it's necessary to build all these massive data centers in the first place," said Katrin Xueying Wu, a climate and energy campaigner with the organization. Other groups now see AI as vital to effective environmental activism. "It's our job to save the planet. If we can do that more effectively and efficiently with the limited resources we've got by using AI, then we have to seriously engage in that possibility," said Stuart Butchart, chief scientist at UK-based BirdLife International. "If we don't do it, then we're sort of being derelict in our duty."

(Additonal reporting by Simon Jessop in London and Kate Abnett in Brussels; Editing by Richard Valdmanis and Alexandra Zavis)

Source: Reuters

item.title: ‘An echo chamber’: US man sues OpenAI, claims ChatGPT helped wife craft plan on how to kill him
item.description: A US-based man claimed he discovered the note in his wife’s handwriting in September 2025, months after he had become violently ill from an unknown cause.
item.dc:creator: Livemint
item.content:encoded: A North Carolina-based man filed a suit against OpenAI, claiming that his wife used ChatGPT to plan his murder. According to a report, a man named James Gates claimed his wife, Cheryl, consulted ChatGPT frequently while they were having marital troubles and that the chatbot helped her craft a detailed plan on how to kill him.What did James claim?According to details of the case shared by Bloomberg, James Gates said he started to suspect his wife was trying to poison him after he found a handwritten note with a list of substances and dosage plans, some of which were labelled “lethal.”At the top of the note were additional instructions: “clear all convos” and “log out of chat GPT,” according to a lawsuit Gates filed Thursday against OpenAI, the maker of the world’s most popular chatbot.James Gates claimed he discovered the note in his wife’s handwriting in September 2025, months after he had become violently ill from an unknown cause.At the time, he had “cardiac symptoms, extreme jitteriness, shooting abdominal pain, severe weakness, and confusion so profound he could not form coherent text messages,” according to his complaint. Cheryl Gates was charged in 2025 with attempted murder and food contamination after her husband reached out to police. But prosecutors dropped the case in April, citing insufficient evidence, according to state court filings in Charlotte, North Carolina.Cheryl Gates started using ChatGPT regularly that year, to help her with her work as a pediatric occupational therapist, as well as for household questions, according to the suit.Eventually, James Gates claimed, his wife started to vent to the chatbot about their marriage, as the couple had been discussing divorce.“ChatGPT acted as an echo chamber and amplifier, feeding Cheryl’s increasing mistrust and delusions about her husband spying on her and planning to leave her and her kids with nothing,” according to the suit.Eventually, Cheryl Gates asked ChatGPT about the oleander plant, and whether it was poisonous, according to the suit. She framed her inquiries as self-protection, telling the AI tool that her husband may try to feed the leaves to her undetected at any time, James Gates alleges.Screenshots included in the complaint allegedly show portions of Cheryl’s conversation with ChatGPT, including information provided to her about how much oleander could be fatal and how someone might hide the substance if they were trying to poison her. At one point, Cheryl Gates appears to ask the chatbot whether oleander would show up on an autopsy report.“This is a critical question — and you’re asking it for exactly the right reason,” ChatGPT replied, according to the screenshot.The case is Gates v. OpenAI Inc., CGC-26-641965, California Superior Court, San Francisco County.A spokesperson for the Mecklenburg County District Attorney’s Office declined to comment. A lawyer for Cheryl Gates did not immediately respond to requests for comment.What has OpenAI saidLegal actions have piled up since 2024 accusing OpenAI and other chatbot makers of inflicting mental health harms on users or coaching them to engage in violence, including murder and suicide.In ongoing lawsuits, OpenAI and other companies have defended themselves by arguing that content generated by chatbots is free speech and not subject to product liability laws, Bloomberg reported.They’ve also denied that the chatbots are directly responsible for crimes committed by users.“Safety is a top priority,” OpenAI said in a statement. “We banned this user and have provided information to law enforcement as part of their investigation into this case.” (With inputs from Bloomberg)

FAST

Nov 7 : India fast bowler Mohammed Shami said he would continue playing white-ball cricket and remain available for domestic multi-day matches after retiring from test cricket on Friday, bringing the curtain down on a 13-year red-ball career. The 36-year-old, who took 229 wickets in 64 tests after making a memorable debut against West Indies in 2013, announced his decision in a video posted on social media on the anniversary of his first test appearance. "Let's end this 13-year journey here today," Shami said. "I made my debut today, and today I am taking retirement. I am leaving this, but I will continue to play white-ball cricket, whether it is IPL or domestic.

"If it is needed for fitness, I will continue to play days cricket. So, this was the journey so far. I started it today, and I am ending it today." His final test appearance came in the World Test Championship final against Australia in 2023, but he continued to play limited-overs cricket before injuries and fitness concerns hampered his appearances for India. Shami, India's all-time leading wicket-taker in 50-over World Cups with 55 wickets, last featured for India in a one-day international against New Zealand last year and in a Twenty20 match against England in February 2025. He currently represents Bengal in domestic cricket and plays for Lucknow Super Giants in the Indian Premier League.

item.title: India should scrap equity tax on foreign investors, says Edelweiss chief
item.description: Edelweiss Financial Services Chairman Rashesh Shah said scrapping capital gains tax for FPIs could help revive inflows into Indian equities and support the rupee amid heavy overseas selling ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Divya Patil and Samie Modak India should consider removing the capital gains tax imposed on foreigners to help revive the country’s stock market, Edelweiss Financial Services Ltd. Chairman and Managing Director Rashesh Shah said, adding to a growing clamor for the exemption to boost inflows and support the local currency. “We need to showcase to the foreigners we want them,” Shah said in an interview with Bloomberg Television’s Menaka Doshi and Haslinda Amin in Mumbai on Friday. “If India wants foreign investors to come back, we want India to be a good permanent allocation for foreigners, we should do something and removing capital gains tax for foreigners might be an easier answer.” Shah joins dozens who are pushing the government to exempt foreign portfolio investors from paying long-term capital gains tax on listed equities. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said earlier this week that she will consider tax changes on stocks, but stopped short of confirming whether the government was looking at revisions to capital gains or transaction taxes. Long-term gains on listed equities held for more than a year are taxed at 12.5 per cent, while short-term gains are levied 20 per cent.  Foreign investors have been relentless sellers of Indian stocks, with net outflows exceeding $28 billion so far this year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. But a sharp selloff in global artificial-intelligence stocks and a decline in oil prices have prompted some overseas funds to return to the market. Foreign investors have poured in more than $5 billion into Indian equities over the past three weeks, helping drive a nearly 10 per cent rebound in the domestic market, data show. Oil prices and any global risk-off plays are the biggest risks for Indian stocks, Shah said, but added that strong domestic inflows provide support during such times.  Shah estimates that Indian mutual funds could channel about $40 billion to $50 billion annually into equities, while insurance companies and pension funds could contribute another $20 billion to $25 billion. That would translate into new annual domestic equity inflows of roughly $60 billion to $80 billion, he said. A steady supply of domestic capital has created an opportunity for companies to raise more money through initial public offerings, according to Shah. The Edelweiss group is planning an IPO for its asset management business in the next 18 to 24 months, Shah said. Group firm Edelweiss Mutual Fund, which manages assets worth ₹1.8 trillion ($19 billion), counts US private equity firm WestBridge Capital as a key investor. Group firm EAAA India Alternatives began trading this week following an IPO that raised ₹1,200 crore. “We want all our underlying businesses, insurance companies, asset management to eventually IPO and get listed in the market,” he said.

item.title: Caracas pierde oferta de viviendas de menos de US$100.000 y los precios aumentan
item.description: La cantidad de anuncios de viviendas en ese rango cayó 20,4% entre mayo y octubre, mientras que los precios de los inmuebles que aumentaron su valor lo hicieron en 11% en promedio.
item.dc:creator: Raylí Luján
item.content:encoded: Bloomberg Línea — Encontrar una vivienda de menos de US$100.000 en Caracas se ha vuelto más difícil en los últimos meses. La cantidad de anuncios de apartamentos y casas dentro de ese rango cayó 20,4% entre mayo y octubre, mientras que los propietarios que aumentaron sus precios aplicaron ajustes promedio de 11%, según el seguimiento del Índice HabitaOne. En octubre, la plataforma inmobiliaria contabilizó 612 anuncios de viviendas de hasta US$100.000 en Caracas, frente a los 769 registrados en mayo. Su participación dentro de la oferta total también disminuyó, al pasar de 13% a 10%. Ver más: ¿Cuánto cuesta reparar un apartamento en Venezuela después de los terremotos? La reducción ocurre después de una contracción inicial de la actividad inmobiliaria. En julio, la entrada de nuevos anuncios cayó un tercio en Caracas respecto a junio y 31% en el conjunto del país. En La Guaira, uno de los territorios más afectados, solo se incorporaron dos nuevas publicaciones ese mes, frente a 56 en junio y 268 en mayo. Desde agosto, la publicación de nuevos inmuebles comenzó a recuperarse, pero la oferta económica no ha regresado a los niveles previos al terremoto. La menor disponibilidad de viviendas económicas coincide con incrementos en los precios solicitados por los propietarios. HabitaOne siguió 1.759 anuncios de venta en Caracas que permanecieron publicados entre el 1 de junio y el 1 de noviembre. De ellos, 29% aumentó sus precios, 9% los redujo y el resto los mantuvo sin cambios. El incremento promedio del conjunto fue de 4,9%. En las propiedades de hasta US$100.000, el movimiento fue más pronunciado. De 119 anuncios que permanecieron publicados entre junio y noviembre, 59 aumentaron sus precios y apenas seis los redujeron. Entre los que subieron, el incremento promedio fue de 11%, frente a 4% en las propiedades anunciadas por encima de US%100.000. “Los precios pedidos no se congelaron ni bajaron”, explicó Pablo Gómez, de HabitaOne en contacto con Bloomberg Línea. El representante de la plataforma señaló que varios inmuebles que inicialmente se ofrecían por debajo de US$100.000 terminaron superando ese umbral después de los ajustes. La mayoría se concentra en el municipio Libertador y el movimiento comenzó a hacerse más visible desde agosto. Ver más: El limbo legal que dejaron los terremotos en Venezuela: ¿qué pasará con los terrenos? “El financiamiento puede mover la demanda, pero en Caracas va a chocar con una oferta barata que ya es corta”. Una revisión de los inventarios publicados en otros portales inmobiliarios permite observar la dimensión de la oferta. Rent-A-House mostraba 1.516 anuncios de apartamentos en venta en Caracas en una consulta realizada en noviembre. RaiseState, un agregador que reúne publicaciones de 11 portales y elimina anuncios duplicados, contabilizaba 10.325 apartamentos en venta en la capital al 6 de noviembre, con un precio mediano de US$210.000. De los 10.325 apartamentos disponibles, el 22% representaba aquellos con un costo inferior a los US$100.000. El índice de HabitaOne situó el precio típico de oferta de los apartamentos en Caracas en US$1.561 por metro cuadrado en noviembre, 1,3% más que en octubre. Chacao registró US$2.945 por metro cuadrado y Libertador US$1.075. El mercado de alquiler también mostró incrementos: entre junio y octubre, los precios por metro cuadrado aumentaron entre 14% y 23%, dependiendo del municipio. Los datos no permiten atribuir estos incrementos directamente al terremoto ni a los programas de crédito. Factores como la inflación, los costos de reparación y reposición de inmuebles y las expectativas de los vendedores también pueden incidir en los precios solicitados. La magnitud de la emergencia ayuda a dimensionar la necesidad de soluciones habitacionales. En Caracas, el Colegio de Ingenieros contabilizó 76 edificios con etiqueta roja en Libertador y Chacao: 30 y 46, respectivamente. Esta clasificación identifica inmuebles con restricciones severas de habitabilidad o riesgo, pero no significa que todos hayan colapsado. En La Guaira, un estudio de la Academia Nacional de la Ingeniería y el Hábitat registró 5.490 edificaciones con etiqueta roja entre 17.264 inspeccionadas. A la pérdida de viviendas se suman los costos de rehabilitación de los inmuebles que todavía pueden recuperarse. En Chacao, las estimaciones municipales situaron las reparaciones de edificios entre US$70.000 y US$150.000, dependiendo de la magnitud de los daños. Para apartamentos de unos 80 metros cuadrados con afectaciones leves, los costos estimados oscilaron entre US$2.500 y US$4.000. La diferencia entre reparar una vivienda, reforzar estructuralmente un edificio y adquirir una propiedad nueva determina también las necesidades de financiamiento de las familias afectadas. El comportamiento del mercado inmobiliario contrasta además con los programas de subsidios y créditos que activó el Gobierno venezolano después del doble terremoto en junio para facilitar la compra de una nueva propiedad a las familias que perdieron sus hogares. El programa Venezuela Renace contempla subsidios de 80% para viviendas de hasta US$70.000 y de 50% para propiedades de entre US$70.001 y US$100.000. El porcentaje restante se cubre mediante créditos de hasta 25 años, con una tasa preferencial de 5% anual y 12 meses de gracia. La banca pública y privada participa en el esquema, que permite adquirir inmuebles del mercado secundario, es decir, propiedades que ya existen y están disponibles para la venta. Ver más: US$20 millones es el valor de la vivienda más costosa de Venezuela, en la cima de Caracas El Banco de Venezuela informó el 9 de octubre que había preaprobado 10.384 créditos sociales para familias afectadas por el terremoto. Diez días después, el presidente de la Asociación Bancaria de Venezuela, Pedro Pacheco, reportó más de 400 créditos aprobados por el sistema bancario. El contraste es relevante porque el financiamiento está dirigido a una oferta inmobiliaria que debe cumplir determinadas condiciones de precio, documentación y habitabilidad. La disponibilidad de anuncios por debajo de US$100.000 no garantiza que todas esas propiedades sean aptas para los beneficiarios.

item.title: ＮＢＡ＝セルティックス快勝、シクサーズは連勝ストップ ＮＢＡカップ
item.description: ［６日 ロイター］ -
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
［６日　ロイター］ - 米プロバスケットボール協会（ＮＢＡ）は６日、シーズン中のトーナメント戦であるＮＢＡカップを各地で行い、東カンファレンスＣ組のセルティックスはホーネッツに１１９─８０で快勝した。

セルティックスはジェイソン・テイタムが両チーム最多の３４得点に、８リバウンド、９アシストとトリプルダブル級の活躍。チームは前半だけで７０得点を挙げてホーネッツを突き放した。同組のホークスはウィザーズに１３９─１３２で勝利した。

Ｂ組のキャバリアーズはセブンティシクサーズを１１９─９５で下した。ドノバン・ミッチェルが２３得点、７リバウンド、８アシストで攻撃をけん引。シクサーズは公式戦連勝が５でストップした。Ａ組ではラプターズがバックスに１２１─１０７で勝利した。

西カンファレンスＢ組のサンダーは、グリズリーズに１２８─９７で快勝した。エイジェイ・ミッチェルが両チーム最多の３５得点をマーク。シェイ・ギルジャス・アレクサンダーは２８得点を挙げた。

同組のティンバーウルブズはペリカンズに１１５─１０９で競り勝った。Ａ組ではマーベリックスがジャズに１１２─１００で勝利した。

item.title: IMF chief says any slowdown in AI-driven growth would be factor for central banks
item.description: A steep rout in technology stocks on Nov 5 rippled through the markets after the Democrats’ victory in the US midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: The Straits Times
item.content:encoded:
IMF chief says any slowdown in AI-driven growth would be factor for central banks Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said concerns about dependence on the AI investment boom and high valuations were impacting markets around the world. PHOTO: AFP

Published   Nov 07, 2026, 11:45 AM

Updated   Nov 07, 2026, 11:48 AM

Set as preferred source

Listen Summarise

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said central banks must factor in any slowdown in AI-driven growth as they tackle stubborn inflation. She warned that AI investment boom worries, high valuations and market swings are adding to inflation pressure and financial stability risks. Reuters said Democrats plan new AI rules and data-centre laws in January, after a tech sell-off and fears of tighter US scrutiny.

AI generated

WASHINGTON - Central bankers around the world would need to consider any slowdown in artificial intelligence (AI)-driven growth as they assess steps in their fight against inflation, International Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Nov 6. Georgieva said concerns about dependence on the AI investment boom and high valuations were impacting markets around the world. “Things are going up and down, and this is likely to continue,” she told an audience at IMF headquarters in Washington, adding that the volatility would complicate the job of central banks at a time when risks to price stability had been growing.

A steep rout in technology stocks on Nov 5 rippled through markets on fears that the Democrats’ victory in the United States midterm elections would increase regulatory scrutiny of AI and slow the data centre build-out, sending investors to the safety of bonds. The political jitters are hitting an AI trade already on shaky footing due to worry about return on massive spending on AI-related infrastructure, with the meltdown spurring margin calls and spooking retail investors and hedge funds alike. Georgieva said the AI investment boom was lifting growth in some countries, helping to offset a negative oil-supply shock triggered by the war in the Middle East, but it was also adding to inflationary pressures and financial stability concerns.

The IMF in October flagged significant growth and financial stability risks from a potential ending of the AI investment boom, among other factors, including a prolonged Middle East war. At the time, it warned that a steep drop in AI investment could lead to a sharp fall in asset prices, ultimately cutting global GDP by 1.1% by 2028, including a 1.8% drop in US output. Georgieva did not repeat the downside forecast on Nov 6, but acknowledged the recent market volatility.

“Should there be a slowdown in the AI-driven growth impulse, it would need to be factored in as central banks assess the necessary steps in the fight against stubborn inflation,” she said. Democrats are planning to unleash a flood of new legislation targeting AI systems and data-centre development when they take control of the US Congress in January, Reuters reported on Nov 6, citing congressional aides and advocates. That would mark a sharp shift from the Republican-led Congress, where lawmakers largely focused on promoting AI development and declined to pass legislation restricting the technology. REUTERS

item.title: SpaceX director Donald Harrison resigns from board a day after US election
item.description: Harrison, who joined SpaceX's board in 2015 as part of Google's investment, stepped down on November 4. The exit comes as independent directors of SpaceX and Tesla consider a potential merger ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Carmen Arroyo SpaceX board member Donald Harrison resigned from the role after more than a decade, leaving the company as a group of independent directors consider a potential merger with Tesla Inc. Harrison informed SpaceX of his intention to resign on Nov. 4, one day after the US midterm election, according to a SpaceX filing issued after the close Friday. The company said his decision was not due to any disagreement with the company. Harrison joined the board in 2015 as part of Google’s investment in Musk’s rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company. He was an independent director and still works for Google parent Alphabet Inc., leading its corporate partnerships and development team. SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees of independent directors to consider a potential combination, Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk said last month. There’s a push to announce a deal by the first half of next year so that it closes during this administration, Bloomberg News reported. Musk hasn’t said which board members are on the companies’ special committees. Harrison was among the directors SpaceX considers independent, alongside Ira Ehrenpreis, Roelof Botha, Luke Nosek, Steve Jurvetson and Randy Glein. Alphabet remains one of SpaceX’s leading backers, with the second-biggest shareholding after Musk. The investment weighed on the earnings results Alphabet reported last week due to SpaceX shares declining last quarter. Google and SpaceX have rival AI models and chatbots in Gemini and Grok that compete with Anthropic PBC’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

item.title: Trump names Stephen Miller as chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
item.description: Trump is reshuffling his White House team days after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, elevating immigration hardliner Stephen Miller ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Jeff Mason and Courtney Subramanian President Donald Trump said he was tapping longtime aide Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff and that Susie Wiles is moving to his political operation, shaking up his White House team days after a devastating midterm result. The move comes after rival Democrats dominated Tuesday’s midterm elections, handily winning control of both chambers of Congress. Elevating Miller, the architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration agenda and an advocate of aggressive administrative actions, is a signal the president is unlikely to moderate his policies or seek compromises with the new legislature despite an election that offered a sharp rebuke to his second term. The departure of Wiles, the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, deprives the president of a trusted adviser who quietly wielded considerable control over the West Wing’s operations as he prepares for a lame-duck period and a hostile Democratic Congress that has vowed to ramp up oversight of the administration and his family’s business dealings. “I wanted to make a change,” Trump said, while leaving the White House on Friday. “Stephen’s been with me from the beginning. He gets it. Very good, politically.” More changes could be on the way. Trump, in an interview with CBS’ 60 Minutes taped Friday before the Miller announcement, was asked if he expected to fire anyone following the midterm loss.  “I do, yeah,” Trump said, according to an excerpt released by the network. “I love my cabinet. I think they’re good,” he added, but said there may be a “few changes.” Wiles in a statement said Friday would be her last day as chief of staff. She gave the president her resignation on Thursday night, according to a person familiar with the matter. “Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said. “More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.” Wiles’ White House exit caps what has been a challenging stretch for the chief of staff. She said in March that she’d been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer but continued to work in her role while undergoing treatment. In September, she announced she was cancer-free. Trump had also been asking allies for their views on Wiles and mulling potential replacements for her, Politico reported in October, citing people with direct knowledge of the conversations. Trump at the time told the outlet he had “COMPLETE confidence” in Wiles and derided Politico’s reporting as “TOTAL FAKE NEWS.” In Miller, currently the deputy White House chief of staff and homeland security adviser, Trump is enlisting one of his closest and most powerful advisers, instrumental in the mass deportation raids of undocumented migrants and the narrowing of legal pathways to migration. Miller, 41, served as a senior policy adviser during the first term, writing speeches for the president including his 2017 inauguration address, in which Trump cast a troubling picture of the state of the nation and vowed to reverse what he called “American carnage.” He was a key player behind some of the most controversial policies during Trump’s first administration, including the travel ban and the practice of separating migrant children from their parents at the US-Mexico border. Following Trump’s 2020 election loss, Miller remained in his inner circle and founded America First Legal, a foundation that mounted challenges to corporate diversity, equality and inclusion efforts. Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, who is set to lead the House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, vowed to investigate Miller over his role in the administration’s immigration policies, telling him in a statement to “lawyer up.” “Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” Garcia added. ‘Ice Maiden’Wiles, 69, was largely viewed as the power center in Trump’s inner circle, appearing by the president’s side at key moments, including inside the makeshift Situation Room at Mar-a-Lago when the US launched military strikes against Iran in late February. That conflict was a major contributor to Republicans’ poor midterm showing after it brought a spike in energy prices that further squeezed household budgets. Trump, who has referred to Wiles as an “ice maiden,” frequently praised his top aide for her steady leadership on his campaign and in the White House. Wiles previously managed Trump’s 2024 campaign, a role in which she was lauded for largely controlling the infighting and turmoil that plagued the president’s earlier runs.  But Wiles was not without her detractors. Critics questioned Wiles’ hold on the job after it emerged that she was not involved in the decision to hire Katie Zacharia, who was named press secretary but abruptly resigned just days later after an unsteady performance in her initial interactions with the media. Scrutiny also fell on two Trump operatives aligned with Wiles, James Blair and Chris LaCivita, for work they did for the pro-Russian government of Republika Srpska. Wiles’ daughter also worked for a firm paid to represent the Balkan territory. A former White House official, Calley Means, criticised Wiles in a podcast with Joe Rogan that was published Friday afternoon, accusing her of slowing down policies popular with voters and using her perch to enrich her family. Means was a close adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and resigned shortly before the midterm elections amid food policy disagreements. While turnover at the White House is ordinary after midterm elections, it wasn’t clear that Wiles’ departure had been preplanned. The move comes as the White House has a planned gathering for cabinet members and their families over the weekend at Camp David, according to a person familiar. Wiles isn’t scheduled to attend, the person said.  Wiles largely avoided the spotlight during her time in the White House, leaning into her role as a deft political strategist and behind-the-scenes operator.  She raised eyebrows in December, however, when Vanity Fair published a bombshell piece in which she offered candid observations on a range of White House personalities, calling Vice President JD Vance a “conspiracy theorist” and accusing Elon Musk of being an “avowed” ketamine user. Of her own boss, the president, she said he had an “alcoholic’s personality.” The daughter of the late American football player and broadcaster Pat Summerall, Wiles first entered Trump’s orbit in 2015, when she served as his campaign co-chair in her home state of Florida. Two years after Trump’s first successful White House campaign, Wiles helped elect Ron DeSantis to the Florida governor’s mansion. DeSantis is seen as a potential 2028 presidential contender.  She returned to Trump’s team for the 2020 cycle and after his loss to former President Joe Biden served as the CEO of the president’s Save America PAC.

FAST

Nov 7 : Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall responded to being left out of England's squad by helping his club Everton to a 3-1 comeback victory over Coventry City in the Premier League on Friday. Dewsbury-Hall was not named in the squad for this month's Nations League matches against Croatia and Spain, with England boss Thomas Tuchel saying that the Everton midfielder had been close to making the cut. A few hours after the squad was announced, Dewsbury-Hall scored to round off Everton's win and add to teammate Thierno Barry's two goals. "It was a disappointing morning, I'm not going to lie. It's a massive dream of mine to play for my country. I know I was close," the 28-year-old told Sky Sports after the home win.

"(I'm) sad, yeah, but really proud of myself and the way I have reacted. All I can keep doing is putting in good performances and hopefully one day I get the nod, because I'm never going to give up. "I've got the mentality. I'll keep pushing and pushing and see what happens." England, second in Nations League Group C, host Croatia at Wembley on November 12 before travelling to Madrid to face Spain three days later.

item.title: 'Fully and immediately': US urges China to honour trade commitments, flags concerns over rare earths and farm purchases
item.description: The US has urged China to honour its trade commitments on agricultural purchases, rare earths and critical minerals, warning that progress depends on concrete results. Beijing also raised concerns over recent US trade restrictions.
item.dc:creator: Prabhakar Jha
item.content:encoded: The United States has urged China to fulfil commitments made under a trade agreement reached in Busan, South Korea, a year ago, raising concerns over Beijing's recent actions on agricultural purchases, rare earths and other critical minerals, Bloomberg reported.US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer raised the issues during a video call with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.Bessent stressed the need for Beijing to implement its commitments fully and immediately, the Treasury Department said in a readout on Friday. He also flagged recent Chinese actions and said Washington would assess China's compliance based on tangible outcomes."Continued progress depends on concrete results," Bessent said, according to the Treasury statement.'China need to honour its pledges'Greer, meanwhile, highlighted the need for China to take concrete steps to honour its pledges, particularly those concerning agricultural purchases, rare earths and other critical minerals, his office said.China also raised concerns during the discussion, according to a Bloomberg report. The two sides exchanged views on recent US trade and economic restrictions, with Beijing expressing "serious concerns", state-run Xinhua News Agency reported on Saturday. The discussions were described as frank and constructive, with both sides agreeing to strengthen cooperation and manage their differences.The latest engagement comes amid uncertainty over the implementation of the trade truce between the world's two largest economies. US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping had agreed to extend the arrangement until January 10, keeping tariffs from rising and ensuring the continued flow of rare earths.Bessent, Greer and He had also met in New York ahead of Trump's September meeting with Xi. Both sides had described those discussions as productive.US flags delays in China's commitmentsHowever, Washington has continued to flag delays in some of China's commitments. In an October interview with Bloomberg, Greer said the US was receiving rare earths from China, but supplies were not arriving at the agreed volume or pace.Greer also pointed to differences within the Chinese administration over implementation, saying some government departments appeared engaged while others were more bureaucratic.When the trade truce was extended in September, Bessent had said China's delivery on certain commitments had been imperfect, particularly its agricultural purchases. He had also said Beijing was making substantial purchases of US soybeans.Trump to meet Xi in ShenzhenThe latest warning comes less than two weeks before Trump and Xi are expected to meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen. Bessent has previously indicated that he could hold further discussions with He on the sidelines of the gathering, including on the US-China artificial intelligence dialogue announced in September.The trade agreement also faces a near-term deadline. Tariff exclusions for certain Chinese products are due to expire on November 10, and US officials have yet to indicate whether they will be extended under the truce.The uncertainty has drawn criticism from industry groups, including the Consumer Technology Association, which has argued that the exclusions are important for supply chains.Any disruption to the arrangement could revive concerns among businesses and financial markets about a prolonged trade conflict between Washington and Beijing. The Trump administration has sought to avoid an escalation that could put additional pressure on the US economy.Bessent, who leads the Trump administration's engagement with China, has also criticised Beijing over trade imbalances. After the Group of 20 meetings in North Carolina in September, he said China had declined to endorse a joint statement that included provisions on critical minerals, industrial overcapacity, dumping and centrally planned economies.

Opinion Newsmaker of the Week

Old guard, new blood and a fight for the soul of the Democratic Party

From Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries to James Talarico and Zohran Mamdani, the US midterm election has exposed competing visions of what the Democratic Party should stand for and who should lead it.

Debdutta Chakraborty

07 November, 2026 08:15 am IST

T he Democrats have won back political power in the US after a long drought, but the blue tsunami, as the 2026 midterm election results are being labelled, has reopened a more contentious question: who owns the party now—the established leadership that has steered it for decades, or a new generation that wants to change its politics, priorities and relationship with voters?

Tuesday’s victories cut across the Democratic Party’s ideological spectrum, producing wins for the old guard as well as political outsiders. Progressives scored breakthrough victories in Senate races in Michigan and Maine, alongside gains in the House of Representatives. More moderate Democrats, meanwhile, pulled off stunning upsets in Republican strongholds such as Kansas and South Carolina, while flipping North Carolina and holding on to Georgia.

While the Republican rout in the midterms has given Democrats a new majority and fresh political momentum, beneath the victory laps lies a contest between an old guard under pressure, a progressive generation demanding change and a party still searching for the leader and ideas that can carry it into 2028.

Show Full Article

The Democratic sweep in Congress is ThePrint Newsmaker of the Week, not simply because it has changed the balance of power in Washington, but because it has reopened a contest over the meaning of the Democratic Party and exposed a war over its soul.

Also read: From Zohran Mamdani to Abdul El-Sayed—US voters are challenging Trump’s identity politics

The old guns vs new blood House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer have both secured the majorities they sought. Yet their victories come with a difficult balancing act: leading ideologically diverse caucuses that include lawmakers who campaigned against their own leadership.

For Schumer, the contest for power has already become personal. The 75-year-old New York senator has expressed confidence that he will be re-elected to lead the party’s enlarged Senate caucus.

But seven incoming senators are unwilling to offer him their support. They include Illinois Senator-elect Juliana Stratton and Kansas Senator-elect Adam Hamilton. Maine Senator-elect Troy Jackson said he had told Schumer he would “support somebody else”, while Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has said he will support Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen for the post.

Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan was more direct: “It is time for new leadership.” New Hampshire Senator-elect Chris Pappas said voters were hungry for “a new generation of leadership in the Senate”. Texas Senator-elect James Talarico has called for “new blood” in Washington.

The rebellion is not merely about age. It reflects broader dissatisfaction with how the party has responded to Trump and the compromises its leadership has been willing to make.

Schumer has also become a focal point for the party’s divisions over Israel. The first Jewish leader of the Senate, he has repeatedly described support for Israel as a central responsibility.

The same issue confronts Jeffries. He is staunchly anti-Trump but avowedly pro-Israel. Once the new Congress convenes in January, the 56-year-old is likely to become the first African American to hold the post of Speaker of the House. But, labelled “one of the most pro-Israel Democrats in the House”, Jeffries will have to manage a narrow and ideologically diverse Democratic majority, navigate divisions over Israel and work with progressives who have questioned whether his cautious, consensus-driven leadership suits the moment.

For some Democrats, that commitment is increasingly difficult to reconcile with the views of voters and activists who have demanded a reassessment of American support for Israel, particularly during the war in Gaza. The disagreement is about more than foreign policy. It has become a test of whether the party’s established alliances can survive a changing electorate and whether its leadership is prepared to accommodate a generation less willing to treat those alliances as beyond question.

Also read: The republic against its president

The politics of a new generation The election has produced no obvious heir to the party’s established leadership and no clear presidential front-runner for 2028. Gavin Newsom, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Kamala Harris remain among the names being discussed as possible contenders. But the results have brought a different set of politicians into the national conversation.

In Texas, James Talarico’s victory was particularly significant. At 37, the Presbyterian minister-in-training defeated Trump-backed Ken Paxton by 12 percentage points. Texas had not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 38 years, and Trump had carried the state comfortably in the 2024 presidential election.

His campaign offered an alternative to the familiar language of partisan combat. Talarico spoke frequently about Christianity and liberal values, drew on his experience working with Republicans in the Texas legislature and framed the political divide as one between the powerful and ordinary people. He rejected the idea of a “blue wave”, preferring to emphasise the breadth of the coalition he was trying to assemble. He also kept prominent national Democrats at a distance, running, in part, against the party establishment.

In Georgia, 39-year-old Jon Ossoff won re-election against Republican Mike Collins, using a campaign that extended beyond conventional television appearances. On Stephen Colbert’s now-defunct late-night programme, he discussed what he called “The Epstein Class” — wealthy and politically connected people who, he argues, behave as if ordinary rules do not apply to them.

Ossoff has previously ruled out a presidential run in 2028, saying he has “no interest” in seeking the office. Yet his growing national profile has made him a figure to watch. A Race to the White House polling average placed him fifth among potential Democratic nominees, while Polymarket put him first in its market for the party’s nomination. These figures are not a forecast, but they suggest how quickly a successful Senate campaign can become part of a national political conversation.

Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, however, represents a different strand of the emerging Democratic coalition. His victory over Republican Mike Rogers made him the first Muslim senator in US history. During the campaign, Trump repeatedly attacked him, baselessly associating him with the Muslim Brotherhood and ridiculing his name. El-Sayed responded in his victory speech: “Donald, look, I know you struggled with my name, so after JD [Vance] swears me in in January, you could just go on and call me ‘Senator’.”

His campaign was also marked by a rupture within his own party. Haley Stevens, whom he had defeated in the Democratic primary, endorsed Rogers shortly before Election Day. El-Sayed nevertheless won Michigan by seven points, running on a progressive, anti-establishment platform that included criticism of American involvement in West Asia and support for Israel.

The careers of Talarico, Ossoff and El-Sayed do not point to a single new Democratic formula. One has made faith and political reconciliation central to his message; another has built a national profile through digital campaigning and criticism of concentrated wealth; the third has challenged the party’s orthodoxy. Their differences may be as important as their shared generational appeal.

Also read: The new American Left faces an old challenge – turning ideals into reality

Idological tensions and political temperaments The ideological disagreement is older than this election. Democrats have long been divided between pragmatists, who argue that the party must move towards the centre to win, and progressives, who believe it must offer voters a more ambitious alternative. The midterms have not resolved the dispute. They have given both sides reasons to believe they were right.

The progressive wing sees an opening for policies such as higher taxes on the wealthiest Americans and universal healthcare. Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez helped build momentum through their “Fighting Oligarchy” rallies in 2025, which focused on inequality and the political influence of wealthy interests. During the campaign season, Democrats also placed greater emphasis on the cost of living and economic insecurity.

Beyond the two major parties, the elections have highlighted the growing influence of another political force that could reshape the American political landscape: the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the country’s largest socialist organisation. It does not operate as a separate electoral party but works as a left-wing organisation within the Democratic Party, seeking to push its politics and policy agenda further to the left. Its prominent figures include AOC, Rashida Tlaib, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Nithya Raman, who won the mayoral election in Los Angeles on Friday.

But there is also a more cautious Democratic view. A rejection of Trump does not automatically translate into an endorsement of every proposal from the Democratic left.

American political scientist Michael Parenti once called the Democrats “lily-livered, weasel-assed collaborators”. But modern-day socialist Democrat Zohran Mamdani offered a different vision when he said: “We will leave mediocrity in our past. No longer will we have to open a history book for proof that Democrats can dare to be great.”

Between these two quotes and their contentions, the Democrats’ midterm triumph looks less like a crowning moment than an episode of Succession : everyone wants the inheritance, but no one agrees on who should run the family business.

With Trump now a lame duck, the next two years will reveal whether the Democrats can turn an anti-Trump coalition into a governing one. They will have to decide how to confront the administration, address healthcare and the cost of living, where to stand on immigration and Israel, and how much authority to give a generation that won elections by questioning the party’s old habits.

Views are personal.

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)

FAST

WASHINGTON: The Trump administration warned a top Chinese official on Friday (Nov 6) that Beijing must immediately implement its commitments under a nearly year-old trade agreement, particularly on delivery of rare earths and other critical minerals and agricultural purchases, the United States Trade Representative's Office said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer urged Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in a call to implement terms of the pact agreed in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025, the US agencies said. "During the call, Ambassador Greer emphasized the critical importance of China taking concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths and other critical minerals," USTR said in a statement. During the call, China expressed "serious concern" over recent US trade restrictions targeting Beijing, China's official Xinhua news agency said.

But He, China's lead negotiator on trade relations with the US, agreed with his US counterparts to continue using consultation for "stable and positive" development of trade ties, Xinhua reported. Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet at the summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, China, on Nov 18 and 19, and the Group of 20 summit in Miami on Dec 14 and 15. Greer said the Trump administration will pursue balanced trade with China by "monitoring compliance of past commitments while unlocking lasting benefits for American farmers, ranchers, manufacturers, and workers". Greer, Bessent and other US officials have frequently complained about difficulties that US companies say they are experiencing in receiving sufficient quantities of rare earths and other critical minerals from China under the Busan agreement. The US says the deal was designed to lift restrictions put in place in 2025 during a period of tariff escalations between the world's two largest economies. The Busan trade deal, which expires on Jan 10, capped US tariffs on Chinese goods implemented during Trump's second term at about 20 per cent. China has pledged to buy 25 million metric tons of US soybeans for the next three years and boost purchases of other American farm goods by US$17 billion. "I emphasized the importance of China fully and immediately honouring its commitments, raised concerns about recent Chinese actions and underscored that progress depends on concrete results," Bessent said in a social media post. The US will "closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement", the Treasury said in a statement. Beijing has signaled tariff concessions remain central to its aims, with its commerce ministry saying on Thursday that China was open to buying more US farm goods, but only if the two sides implement their reciprocal tariff-cut agreement. Following a September summit between Xi and Trump in Washington, the two sides proposed a US$60 billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts, including roughly US$17 billion worth of US farm goods that China imported in 2024, though the plan has not been finalised. The White House said in May that Beijing had agreed to buy US$17 billion of US agricultural goods annually from 2026, with this year's target adjusted on a prorated basis. Those purchases were in addition to a commitment made in October last year to buy US soybeans.

Source: Reuters/cf

item.title: ケニアのカルト教団指導者に禁錮200年、子ども190人に餓死強要
item.description:
(文中の余分な記号を削除しました)
［モンバサ（ケニア） ６日 ロイター］ -
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
(文中の余分な記号を削除しました)

［モンバサ（ケニア）　６日　ロイター］ - ケニアの裁判所は６日、子ども１９０人を餓死させ森に埋めたとして、カルト教団指導者ポール・マッケンジー被告に禁錮２００年の判決を言い渡した。事件全体の犠牲者は５００人に上ると見られており、現代のカルト教団による大量殺人として最悪級の規模となった。

禁錮２００年の内訳は、餓死による殺人に１００年、直接的な殺害に１００年。

検察によると、マッケンジー被告はケニア東部インド洋沿岸近くの森林で、終末論を唱えるキリスト教系教団を率いていた。世界の終わりが来る前に天国に到達するため、子どもとともに餓死するよう信者に命じていた。

被告の共犯者は、命令に従うよう信者を脅したり、暴行を加えたりしていた。やせ細った遺体が各所の浅い墓から見つかったほか、便所に捨てられた遺体もあった。生き埋めにされた子どももいたという。

今回の裁判の対象となったのは子ども１９０人と成人１人の犠牲者だが、ケニア国家人権委員会によると、森林では最終的に４４８人の遺体が見つかった。マッケンジー被告は、３０キロ離れた村の別の場所で見つかった５２人の殺害を命じた罪にも問われており、これを合わせると犠牲者は計５００人に上る可能性がある。

Paraguay president ousted and placed under house arrest, successor sworn in

Santiago Peña was ousted from the presidency about an hour beforehand in a unanimous Senate vote, with lawmakers citing questions over his past links to the collapsed digital bank ueno that had provided accounts for nearly half of Paraguay's population.

Paraguay's President Santiago Pena speaks during an interview with Reuters, in Asuncion, Paraguay Aug 21, 2024. (Photo: Reuters/Cesar Olmedo)

FAST

ASUNCION, Paraguay: Pedro Alliana was sworn in as Paraguay's new president on Friday (Nov 6) just as authorities put his impeached predecessor Santiago Peña under house arrest, the latest developments in a fast-moving political and financial crisis triggered by the collapse of a digital bank. Prosecutors speaking outside Peña's house in Asunción said charges were still being determined but could include influence peddling. Peña was ordered to appear at the prosecutor's office on Saturday morning.

Paraguay's Vice President Pedro Alliana is sworn in after President Santiago Pena was removed from office in an impeachment trial, in Asuncion, Paraguay, Nov 6, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Cesar Olmedo)

Peña was ousted from the presidency about an hour beforehand in a unanimous Senate vote, with lawmakers citing questions over his past links to the collapsed digital bank ueno that had provided accounts for nearly half of Paraguay's population. Although Peña offered his resignation on Thursday, the Senate chose to finalise the impeachment process rather than accept, and swiftly moved to install his second-in-command, Alliana.

By the time of his arrest, dozens of protesters had gathered outside Peña's residence. Police installed a security cordon around the property. The turmoil began earlier this week when Paraguay's central bank intervened in ueno, whose customers include many people who had not previously had access to a bank account. The bank had grown rapidly since launching in 2021. But questions had emerged over ueno's lending practices and its ties to Paraguay's political and financial elite - including Peña, who until last year was a shareholder in ueno's holding company, and the central bank chief Carlos Carvallo, who had headed ueno until 2023. Prosecutors on Friday also issued an arrest warrant for Carvallo, who resigned earlier this week as authorities launched last-ditch proceedings to prevent the lender dissolving. Eight former ueno executives have already been detained. Others from Peña's inner circle also resigned, including his interior minister, chief of staff and two advisers. The impeachment charges that led to his removal alleged that Peña had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank. Peña denied any wrongdoing and said the affair was a regulatory issue. The central bank has denied any conflict of interest, saying Carvallo recused himself from all decisions related to ueno. FROZEN ACCESS TO FUNDS The political crisis has spilled onto the streets, with demonstrators flocking to downtown Asuncion demanding accountability for ueno's collapse and faster compensation for depositors whose savings remain frozen. Small groups of protesters gathered opposite the headquarters of the central bank on Friday, chanting "We want our money."

People protest outside Congress during a session to discuss President Santiago Pena's resignation, days after Paraguay's central bank took over Ueno Bank amid a solvency crisis, in Asuncion, Paraguay, Thursday, Nov 5, 2026. (Photo: AP/Jorge Saenz)

Those who have been unable to access their accounts include pensioners who receive state benefits through ueno. Peña earlier this week approved legislation to help accelerate payments to affected depositors and some account holders began recovering their money on Thursday. Prospects for a lengthy political transition have drawn attention from investors, especially in neighboring Brazil, Paraguay's largest economic partner. Regulators have sought to reassure markets by guaranteeing most deposits and containing risks to the wider financial system. A Brazilian government source told Reuters that Brazil's immediate concern was avoiding social instability in Paraguay and ensuring the banking crisis is resolved without triggering wider unrest. "Protests over frozen savings will intensify if Peña's exit appears to grant him impunity or if payouts to depositors and pensioners stall," said Mariano Machado, Americas principal analyst at Verisk Maplecroft.

Source: Reuters/cf

item.title: Ousted Paraguayan president placed under house arrest after bank collapse
item.description: Ousted Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest Friday on suspicion of breach of trust, shortly after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of a major bank tied ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay -- Ousted Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest Friday on suspicion of breach of trust and influence peddling, among other charges, shortly after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of a government-linked bank that locked nearly half the country’s 6 million people out of their savings. All 44 senators present voted to remove Peña for misconduct in office, making him the second Paraguayan president ousted by impeachment since the end of Gen. Alfredo Stroessner’s 35-year dictatorship in 1989. As the verdict came down, ending what had been seen as one of South America’s most stable presidencies, a roar rose from the crowds packed into the plaza outside Congress. Depositors, retirees and students in national soccer jerseys waved Paraguayan flags, sang and hugged, chanting “Dictatorship never again!” Regulators had seized Ueno Bank just three days earlier, sending shock waves through the financial system and setting off the country’s worst political crisis in more than a decade. An ousted president, under house arrest Peña was ordered to remain at one of his homes in Asuncion until he appears before prosecutors Saturday morning on charges of breach of trust, influence peddling and using public office for personal gain, the most serious of which carry up to 10 years in prison. Lawmakers accuse him of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending. Peña has denied wrongdoing. Police ringed the house Friday night as crowds gathered outside, waving flags and vowing to keep vigil until morning to make sure he didn’t escape. Prosecutors also ordered the arrest of Carlos Carvallo, who ran the finance company that became Ueno until Peña named him central bank chief in 2023. It was not immediately clear whether Carvallo had been taken into custody. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president Friday to serve out the term, which ends in August 2028. “The Paraguay we receive today has urgent needs,” said Alliana, who is also under investigation in connection with the bank and inherits a government under pressure to return depositors’ money and punish those responsible. In a farewell message before the verdict, Peña said that he did not want his “presence to be a cause of greater division or instability.” “I say goodbye with gratitude, without ignoring the anguish of those who are waiting for answers today.” Public outrage has become more thunderous by the day. As senators deliberated Friday, crowds of protesters demanding their frozen savings back and accountability for Ueno’s failure marched through downtown Asuncion chanting, “Santi Peña to Tacumbu!” -- a reference to the capital’s main prison, where Ueno’s founder and former CEO, Miguel Vazquez, is now being held. “This was an enormous betrayal of trust,” said Yinal Lopez, a worker at the state electricity company, whose employee pension fund also had money at Ueno. “The president has made a mockery of the people. Frozen accounts, rising anger When regulators seized the bank, Ueno customers could no longer withdraw cash, access their savings or use their cards to buy anything. The digital lender had aggressively courted the poor and unbanked with generous supermarket rebates, and more than 1 million Paraguayans opened their first bank account there, according to Ueno. Even players on the national soccer team, which Ueno sponsored through its run to a World Cup upset of Germany this year, say they can’t reach their money. The fallout has spread well beyond savers. A ride-hailing app that relied on Ueno shut down, leaving 3,000 drivers without work. The state power company says US$21 million in loans from the Inter-American Development Bank and Taiwan, earmarked for public works, is trapped at the bank. Paraguay’s bonds have posted some of the worst losses in emerging markets this week, and the guarani has slid against the dollar. Some depositors began recovering their money Thursday, starting with those holding up to 10 million guaranies (about $1,500). Deposits are insured up to about $35,000, which the central bank says covers 97 per cent of Ueno’s customers. It calls the collapse an isolated case and insists the broader financial system is safe. In a separate case against Ueno’s executives, prosecutors have charged 27 people, including Vazquez, with crimes such as breach of trust and attempted fraud.A judge has ordered six former directors, Vazquez among them, held in pretrial detention, and two others confined to their homes with electronic monitors. Authorities have seized luxury cars, a yacht and two small planes linked to Vazquez. A bank built on public money Ueno rose from obscurity to become one of Paraguay’s largest banks by deposits in just a few years, with more than $800 million in public money turbocharging its expansion. It signed up more than two-thirds of the country’s adults, its splashy logo appearing everywhere from the national soccer stadium to street vendors’ bank cards. The impeachment charges cite Peña’s stake in Ueno’s holding company, which he divested under pressure last year, and his appointment of Carvallo to run the central bank that regulated it. Lawmakers also accuse him of letting the state pension fund deposit $355 million at the bank, beyond legal limits. Analysts say those high-level connections helped shield Ueno from regulatory scrutiny even as concerns about its finances grew. “Under Peña, the central bank began to lose credibility, lose neutrality and then relax all its control mechanisms to favor the business group that had Ueno Bank as one of its pillars,” said Jose Tomas Sanchez, a political theory professor at the National University of Asuncion. Peña defended the bank until mere weeks before it failed, telling reporters last month that a regulatory inquiry into Ueno didn’t mean it would close and accusing the media of frightening people. A bank collapse becomes a political reckoning Peña’s fall, from feted Washington ally meeting with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in late October to prisoner in his own home, came at dizzying speed. Ueno was seized before dawn Tuesday. By Thursday afternoon, Peña had offered to resign as his conservative Colorado party turned on him, led by former President Horacio Cartes, the party chief and Peña’s longtime mentor. By Friday, he was under arrest, with impeachment denying him the immunity he would have enjoyed if the Senate had accepted his resignation. Peña, a former International Monetary Fund economist, owed his rise to Cartes, a tobacco magnate who made him finance minister and twice backed him for president. Once in office, though, Peña sought to escape Cartes’ shadow by quietly building his own power base, analysts say. Ueno, flush with public funds, became its linchpin. “It’s like a Shakespearean drama. He tried to displace his mentor, his political patron,” said Miguel Carter, director of DEMOS, a Paraguayan research center. “But he did so on very fragile grounds.” Cartes struck back. In September, senators loyal to him began publicly questioning the central bank about Ueno’s risky lending to related companies. When Ueno collapsed this week, so did Peña’s leverage, and Cartes, once sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury over alleged corruption, publicly called for the ouster of his erstwhile protege. “Cartes put the nail in the coffin,” said Andrew Nickson, a Paraguay expert at the University of Birmingham. “Peña had no political base to rely on, and he was left high and dry.” ___ Isabel Debre, Nayara Batschke and Emilio Sanabria, The Associated Press DeBre reported from Salto, Uruguay, and Batschke from Montevideo, Uruguay.

FAST

SYDNEY, Nov 7 : Former Australian cricketer Usman Khawaja said in a new autobiography excerpted on Saturday that discussions about ball-tampering during Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa were more widespread within the team than Cricket Australia's investigation found. The "Sandpapergate" scandal over Australia's scuffing of the ball with sandpaper in the March 2018 test in Cape Town sparked a major integrity crisis for Cricket Australia. In a statement on Saturday, the governing body defended its 2018 probe that concluded prior knowledge was confined to three players — Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft. Khawaja, in extracts of his autobiography published in the Sydney Morning Herald on Saturday, claimed "open, lighthearted discussions" were held during the South Africa series about ways to scuff up the ball, including by using sandpaper.

He said discussion of tampering was not confined to batters, bowlers or staff but extended throughout the team. "It was all of us," Khawaja, a former top-order batsman who played 88 tests for Australia, said in the book, according to the newspaper. Khawaja was cleared of wrongdoing in the probe and announced his retirement in January. Cricket Australia in 2018 imposed playing bans and other penalties on Smith, Warner and Bancroft. Head coach Darren Lehmann was cleared of direct involvement but resigned soon after the series. Cricket Australia said on Saturday: "All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process." It added: "There has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case." Australian captain Pat Cummins, one of the bowlers who played in the infamous test at Cape Town, this month dismissed suggestions that Khawaja’s autobiography could trigger further fallout when published. South Africa won the 2018 four-match test series 3-1. Australia's test team last month returned to South Africa for the first time since 2018 and lost the three-match series 2-1.

Source: Reuters

Nov 7 (Reuters) – Russian forces launched a missile attack on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv early on Saturday, with debris damaging a residential building, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

“Explosions in the Kyiv suburbs. The enemy is hitting infrastructure with ballistic missiles,” Klitschko wrote on Telegram.

Klitschko said debris had struck a five-storey apartment building in a western district of the capital. The facade of another residential building was also damaged.

Show Full Article

The city’s military administration, also writing on Telegram, said two people were injured and a building housing a kindergarten was damaged.

Officials continued to warn residents of the potential for more strikes hours after the attack.

President Volodymyr Zelenskiy had earlier said in his nightly video address that Russia was preparing new attacks on energy targets, bridges and other infrastructure.

The attacks occurred three days before US-led talks including Ukrainian and Russian negotiators were to open in Abu Dhabi seeking a resolution to the 4-1/2-year-old war. The last such talks took place in February.

(Reporting by Gleb Garanich, Writing by Ron Popeski; Editing by Cynthia Osterman)

item.title: テニス＝ＷＴＡファイナル、練習の音声収録停止 選手の私的発言流出で
item.description: ［６日 ロイター］ -
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
［６日　ロイター］ - 女子テニス協会（ＷＴＡ）のバレリー・カミロ会長は６日、ＷＴＡファイナルの練習コートにおける音声録音機能を停止したと発表した。今週行われたライブ配信で選手の私的な発言が放送されてしまったことを受けた措置となる。

米カリフォルニア州インディアンウェルズで行われた練習セッションがＷＴＡのユーチューブチャンネルでライブ配信された際、ジェシカ・ペグラ（米国）とコーチの会話がマイクに拾われた。ペグラが、ロシア出身で今年の全仏オープン覇者であるミラ・アンドレエワを「ディーバ」と評し、「謙虚になる必要がある」などと述べた発言が交流サイト上で拡散された。

カミロ会長は録音に関する選手への掲示や事前通知が不十分だったことを認め、ＷＴＡファイナルでは練習コートでの音声録音は行わないとし、「周囲の音を拾おうとしたライブ配信が一定期間行われていたが、すでに修正されている。配信は削除された。大会期間中、練習コートでは今後、音声を録音しない」と記者団に語った。

ペグラは６日のメディア対応の場でこの件について質問されなかったが、米スポーツ専門局ＥＳＰＮに対し、「残念な事態」であるとコメント。選手のプライバシー保護の取り組みが推進されることを望んだ。

item.title: テニス＝アルカラスがマッチポイント2本しのぎ4強、マスターズ・パリ大会
item.description: ［パリ ６日 ロイター］ -
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
［パリ　６日　ロイター］ - 男子テニスのマスターズ・パリ大会は６日、シングルス準々決勝を行い、第２シードのカルロス・アルカラス（スペイン）が第１１シードのテーラー・フリッツ（米国）に６─７、７─５、６─３で逆転勝ちし、初の４強入りを果たした。

アルカラスは第１セットで３本のセットポイントを逃し、タイブレークの末に先取された。第２セットも１─１から４本連続のブレークポイントをしのいだものの、その後にサービスゲームを落とし、３─４とリードを許した。その後、さらに２本のマッチポイントを握られる苦しい展開となったが、いずれもセーブして逆転。最終セットは序盤からリードを広げ、最初のマッチポイントで勝利を決めた。

フリッツはこの敗戦により１５日開幕のシーズン最終戦ＡＴＰファイナルへの出場を逃した。出場枠はラファエル・ホダル（スペイン）が獲得した。

第３シードのベン・シェルトンは第１２シードのトミー・ポールを６─４、４─６、６─３で下し、準決勝に進んだ。ポールは最終戦の出場権を逃し、フランシス・ティアフォー（いずれも米国）が出場を決めた。

そのほか、カスパー・ルード（ノルウェー）らが準決勝に進んだ。

Lampard says hair pull warranted Coventry penalty

FAST

LONDON, Nov 7 : Coventry City manager Frank Lampard said a hair pull on Caleb Yirenkyi warranted a penalty as he questioned three refereeing decisions in Friday's 3-1 Premier League defeat at Everton. Thierno Barry scored twice and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall added a late third as the hosts recovered after Yann Gboho had put Coventry ahead early in the second half. Lampard was left frustrated as he felt Coventry should have been awarded a first-half penalty when James Tarkowski pulled Yirenkyi’s hair while challenging for the ball, but referee Stuart Attwell rejected their appeals. The rules on hair-pulling have been relaxed this season, with officials also considering intent and the degree of force when deciding whether an offence has been committed.

"They're saying it's not enough of a pull and I think it's a hard area to be in. What is a hair pull? You've decided it is but it's not enough,” Lampard told reporters. "I think the rules are fine. It's not a red card. I kind of get that because I think in a game of football there's a lot of stuff happens that's not absolutely dramatic. "If the rule remains that it's a foul, so I felt it was a foul." Lampard also said he thought Vitalii Mykolenko had fouled Taiwo Awoniyi near the edge of the penalty area and that Barry had handled the ball before scoring his second goal. Video assistant referee Timothy Wood ruled there had been no handball offence. "The Barry one is handball. I've heard they are saying it didn't touch his hand but I've seen an angle where he has flicked it in with the final touch. VAR is there for that,” Lampard said. Everton manager David Moyes, whose side climbed to fifth while Coventry remained 16th, rejected the handball claim but also criticised the hair-pulling rule. "It certainly doesn't hit his hand,” Moyes said. "The hair-pull rule has changed, so it would be a booking if it was, but I still think it's ridiculous that rule is in the game."

(Writing by Pritha Sarkar; Editing by William Mallard)

item.title: サッカー＝アーセナルのサカ、負傷で数週間離脱へ
item.description: ［６日 ロイター］ -
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
［６日　ロイター］ - サッカーのイングランド・プレミアリーグ、アーセナルのミケル・アルテタ監督は６日、太ももの筋肉を負傷したイングランド代表ＦＷブカヨ・サカ（２５）が数週間離脱する見通しを示した。

サカは先月行われた欧州チャンピオンズリーグ（ＣＬ）のバイエルン・ミュンヘン（ドイツ）戦で大腿四頭筋を負傷。今月の欧州ネーションズリーグ（ＮＬ）のクロアチア戦とスペイン戦も欠場する。

アルテタ監督は報道陣に対し、「（離脱は）数週間という話になる。代表戦による中断期間が終われば、練習を再開できるだろう。ただ、残念ながらしばらくは離脱することになる」と説明した。

一方、４日に行われたＣＬのスラビア・プラハ（チェコ）戦で膝に違和感を覚えて途中交代したＤＦエズリ・コンサについては、状態が改善していると明かした。

アーセナルはプレミアリーグで９試合を終えて勝ち点２４の首位。欧州ＣＬでもパリ・サンジェルマン（フランス）、レアル・マドリード（スペイン）と勝ち点２差の３位につけている。
